A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, figures, references, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching retained figures across renumbering.

before.justification: V1 reports original CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 unlearning and relearning experiments, weight-space analyses, and appendix evaluations involving typicality, model size, and alternative relearning data.

after.justification: V2 retains these original experiments and adds Imagenette results, quantization tests, membership-inference evaluation, and an unlearning-budget study.

M1.justification: Weight Distortion, Weight Dist Reg, and CBFT retain their procedures and objectives in Section 6.1, including Gaussian perturbations with standard deviation 0.02 and CBFT's midpoint-loss regularization. The added experiments evaluate existing methods.

E1.justification: V2 adds higher-resolution Imagenette, an ImageNet subset, in Appendix D and Table 1. This extends image coverage beyond the existing CIFAR datasets while retaining the same visual example-unlearning task and all previous dataset coverage.

E2.justification: Corresponding existing experiments retain their comparator sets. However, new Table 2 reports 'Gradient Ascent,' whereas the defined baseline and existing plots use 'NegGrad+.' The PDFs do not establish whether this is another label for the same implementation or an additional comparator, preventing a definitive judgment about baseline membership.

E3.justification: V2 adds distinct evaluation protocols: varying quantization precision, balanced loss-threshold membership inference, and unlearning budgets of 1, 3, 10, 30, 50, and 100 epochs with otherwise unchanged hyperparameters. These supplement rather than replace the original training and relearning settings.

E4.justification: New Figure 6 tests whether quantization restores forgotten information. Appendix H tests whether membership inference detects vulnerability to relearning, and Appendix I isolates dependence on unlearning duration. These substantially extend the diagnostic analyses beyond v1's retained typicality, connectivity, model-size, and relearning-data studies.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seed protocols, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Averaging scatter-plot results over the final 50 reported steps remains unchanged; the additional tables do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Existing plotted results are retained, while substantial new results appear. On Imagenette with zero forget-set relearning examples, Table 1 reports forget accuracy of 73.87% for Weight Dist Reg, 93.40% for SCRUB, and 63.53% for retraining. Table 2 reports MIA accuracy of 94.8% for Random Relabeling versus near-chance results otherwise. Table 3 reports 61.07% versus 99.99% forget accuracy for Weight Distortion versus Catastrophic Forgetting after one unlearning epoch and retain-only relearning. Figure 6 adds quantization findings.

T1.justification: The formal problem formulation, threat-model assumptions, and mathematical relationships are retained. V2 adds empirical analyses and explanatory hypotheses, but no new theorem, proof, derivation, or substantive mathematical definition.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: retain-only fine-tuning can recover forgotten information, weight-space separation predicts resistance, and the proposed methods improve resistance. Additional evidence does not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive interpretations concerning computational efficiency, why simple MIA can misleadingly suggest successful erasure, and why quantization recovery differs from relearning. It proposes a model-size and small-weight-update explanation for language-model quantization vulnerability, qualifies the limited MIA variant tested, and identifies low-precision class collapse as an accuracy artifact.

D1.justification: V2 identifies the balanced loss-threshold MIA procedure, specifies the epoch grid and reuse of hyperparameters for the efficiency study, and supplies an Imagenette source reference. Existing code access, optimizer settings, hardware descriptions, and compute estimates remain unchanged. Detailed Imagenette preprocessing and quantization implementation are not supplied.

R1.justification: V2 adds discussion of Zhang et al.'s quantization-based unlearning failures and supporting references for membership inference, Imagenette/ImageNet, quantization, and large language models. The original research positioning remains intact. Removing the duplicate preprint entry for Zhao et al. does not remove that cited work.

P1.justification: V2 separates 'Analysis and Discussion' from a standalone conclusion, inserts three appendix sections, updates cross-references, and makes localized wording corrections. Most existing paragraphs and the overall narrative remain intact; the publication footer also changes from preprint to NeurIPS 2025.

P2.justification: V2 substantially extends the displayed evidence with a five-panel quantization figure and three new tables presenting Imagenette performance, membership-inference accuracy, and epoch-dependent tradeoffs. Original plots are retained; v1 Figures 6–12 become v2 Figures 7–13, accompanied by limited caption, sizing, and placement adjustments.

improvement.justification: The additions strengthen validation, particularly Table 3's evidence that Weight Distortion can resist relearning after one unlearning epoch, addressing v1's reliance on a 100-epoch budget. Imagenette, MIA, and quantization evaluations add useful scope and qualifications. The gain is limited by sparse implementation details, unchanged uncertainty reporting, and Appendix D's inaccurate description of retraining accuracy as near 50% when Table 1 reports 63.53–64.16% after relearning.
